strengths: Provides a clear, formalized modular decomposition of MLLM-based active perception into a sensing model M_O and task model M_A, with a principled optimization objective, offering a conceptual framework that could guide future work.

Proposes a dual-form reward (task-aware + heuristic) that is shown via ablation (Table 15) to meaningfully outperform either component alone, and demonstrates that the parallel, single-forward-pass region selection is more efficient than sequential search strategies like GPT-o3's zoom-in or V*.

Constructs and evaluates on a genuinely broad benchmark suite spanning open-world grounding (LVIS small/dense), domain-specific detection (SODA-A aerial, SODA-D driving), and fine-grained interactive segmentation (ThinObjects), demonstrating consistent relative gains across all settings.

Extensive supplementary analyses (appendix) covering robustness to random seeds, comparisons across multiple RL algorithms (PPO, Reinforce++, GMPO, GPG), computational/latency overhead, comparisons to CRG and GPT-5, and diagnostic failure-mode breakdowns, which substantially strengthen the empirical rigor beyond the main text.

Shows that training the sensing policy with perception rewards does not degrade (and sometimes improves) general visual understanding benchmarks (MMBench, MME, RealWorldQA), suggesting active perception can serve as a useful proxy training signal.
Honest and reasonably detailed limitations/future work discussion (Appendix D.1) covering domain gap, fixed action-space size, and lack of memory, along with visualized failure cases.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains very low in several key settings (e.g., APs of 2-4 on LVIS-small, APs around 9 on SODA-A even with the proposed method), raising questions about whether the reported relative improvements translate into practically useful perception capability rather than incremental gains within a still largely unsolved regime.

The central abstract/introduction claim about GPT-o3's zoom-in strategy being inefficient and inaccurate is substantiated only by a single qualitative failure case (Figure 4) and an appendix comparison using GPT-5 (not GPT-o3) on one benchmark; there is no systematic, controlled quantitative comparison against GPT-o3 itself despite it being a central motivating baseline in the abstract and title framing.

The task model M_A is kept fixed while only the sensing policy M_O is optimized, which is a reasonable simplification but somewhat weakens the 'pure RL' framing suggested by the title, and the interactive segmentation results rely on an oracle M_A that simulates perfect feedback, limiting the realism/generalizability of that evaluation.

The framework is restricted to a single-step (T=1), static-image, axis-aligned bounding-box action space; while this is explicitly acknowledged as a simplification, it substantially narrows the scope relative to the general embodied active-perception formulation presented in Section 3, and true sequential/embodied active perception is left unaddressed empirically.

Several important comparisons and robustness analyses (RL algorithm ablation, CRG/GPT-5 comparison, failure diagnostics, latency) are relegated entirely to the appendix, while the main paper's experimental section is comparatively thin on statistical rigor (e.g., no variance/error bars in main tables, single-run numbers) and lacks discussion of why absolute numbers remain low.

Reward design choices (IoU overlap threshold τ=0.3, area range [0.01, 0.5], equal weights λ_i=1) appear heuristically fixed without sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns about how sensitive the method is to these hyperparameters across different datasets/domains.

strengths: Provides a systematic, formal definition of MLLM-based active perception (modular sensing/task decomposition, objective function), giving the field a clearer conceptual vocabulary than prior ad hoc zoom-in heuristics.

Dual-form reward (heuristic + task-aware) is a sensible design to combat reward sparsity in GRPO training, and the ablation (Table 15/16) shows each component contributes to both task performance and preservation of general reasoning ability.
Benchmark coverage is broad: open-world (LVIS small/dense), domain-specific (SODA-A aerial, SODA-D driving), and interactive segmentation (ThinObjects), plus zero-shot transfer to V* VQA tasks.

Extensive appendix ablations (RL algorithm choice, random seeds, reward components, data-combination study, deployment latency, failure-case diagnostics) show an unusually thorough effort to probe robustness and address likely reviewer concerns.

The finding that active-perception RL training does not degrade (and sometimes improves) general VQA/reasoning benchmarks (MMBench, MME, RealWorldQA) is a useful, non-obvious result suggesting active perception could serve as a general proxy task.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains very low across the board (e.g., APs of 2–9 on LVIS/SODA, with the detailed diagnostic in Appendix G.6 showing 554/578 ground-truth objects on LVIS-small are 'complete misses' even for ACTIVE-o3), raising doubts about whether the method is actually solving the active perception problem or merely making marginal improvements over an already weak baseline.

The appendix reference comparison (Table 9) shows GPT-5 + GDINO substantially outperforms ACTIVE-o3 + GDINO (11.3 vs 7.0 APs on LVIS-dense small objects), directly undermining the central claim that a learned, RL-trained sensing policy is needed/superior to a strong off-the-shelf frontier model simply paired with a grounding model; this is not adequately reconciled in the main text.

The RL-algorithm ablation (Table 5) shows GRPO is not uniformly best — GMPO wins on small objects and GPG on large-object recall — undercutting the specificity of the GRPO-centric framing in the main paper, which is relegated to appendix without deeper discussion in the body.

The interactive segmentation evaluation relies on an 'oracle' task model simulating perfect click feedback, which isolates the sensing module but means the reported results (mIoU up to 0.86) do not reflect any realistic end-to-end system, limiting the practical significance of this application.

SODA evaluation uses a non-standard, lowered IoU threshold (0.1 instead of standard 0.5) specifically because standard thresholds yield very low/incomparable scores, which somewhat obscures true detection quality and complicates comparison with the broader small-object-detection literature.

Despite the 'pure reinforcement learning' framing in the title, the method depends heavily on hand-engineered prompts (Figures 2/5/6/7) and manually designed heuristic reward terms (format, overlap, area range, coverage) with fixed weights (all λᵢ=1, untuned), which is a substantial inductive-design component rather than a purely learned behavior.

Training set sizes for domain-specific experiments are small (1,000 images per SODA domain), and no variance/error bars are reported for most main-table results (only one seed study is provided, for a single LVIS-dense setting), limiting confidence in the statistical robustness of the reported gains.

Several claims of novelty (e.g., 'first RL framework for active perception with MLLMs') are only modestly differentiated from closely related prior work (DeepEyes, ZoomEye, V*) — the key distinguishing contribution (parallel vs. sequential region proposals) is a relatively incremental architectural choice rather than a fundamentally new capability.

strengths: Clear and useful formalization of MLLM-based active perception as a sensing/task module decoupling, with a well-motivated single-step parallel-selection instantiation for the 2D static-image setting that is more efficient than sequential zoom-in search (e.g., GPT-o3-style).

The dual-form reward (heuristic + task-aware) is a sensible and empirically validated design; the paper provides thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each reward component (Table 15/16), region-count (Table 12), parallel-vs-sequential sampling (Table 13), and training-data mixtures (Table 14).

Extensive breadth of evaluation across open-world (LVIS small/dense), domain-specific (SODA-A/D aerial and driving), and a different modality (interactive segmentation on ThinObjects), plus zero-shot transfer to V* fine-grained VQA tasks, showing the learned sensing policy generalizes beyond its training objective.

Good engineering rigor in the appendix: robustness across random seeds, comparisons to multiple RL algorithms (PPO, Reinforce++, GMPO, GPG), computational/latency cost breakdowns, and comparisons to a budget-matched CRG baseline and GPT-5-based pipelines.

The method preserves (and slightly improves) general visual understanding/reasoning benchmarks (MMBench, MME, RealWorldQA) despite not training on QA data, suggesting active perception can act as a beneficial auxiliary/proxy objective — a nontrivial and interesting finding.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains very low in several settings (e.g., APs of 2-9 on LVIS/SODA), and the diagnostic analysis itself shows ACTIVE-o3 still completely misses 37% of small targets; the practical utility of the method at this performance level is unclear despite relative gains over weak baselines.

The core comparison motivating the paper (GPT-o3's zoom-in strategy being inefficient/inaccurate) is only supported by a single qualitative failure case (Figure 4/D.5) rather than a quantitative head-to-head benchmark comparison against GPT-o3's actual zoom-in mechanism.

Several domain-specific training sets are quite small (e.g., only 1,000 images sampled from SODA-A/D for training) and evaluation protocols are adapted in non-standard ways (e.g., lowering IoU threshold to 0.1 for SODA due to large domain gap), which weakens confidence in generalizability claims and complicates comparison with prior literature on these benchmarks.

The general embodied-agent formalization (Section 3, multi-step state/action/transition functions) is presented as a core contribution but is never actually instantiated or evaluated beyond the simplified single-step 2D static-image case; the broader claims about active perception for embodied agents are therefore not empirically supported.

The interactive segmentation experiments rely on an oracle task model that simulates perfect click feedback, which isolates the sensing policy but makes it hard to assess real-world end-to-end performance of the proposed framework for this task.

A substantial portion of the strongest supporting evidence (CRG comparison, GPT-5 comparison, latency analysis, failure-mode diagnostics) appears appended post-hoc in the appendix with language suggesting these were added in response to reviewer requests, which raises some concern about the completeness/robustness of the original experimental design.
